messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Akua had always taken pride in her meticulous attention to detail as an architect. She spent years honing her craft, working on high-profile projects, and building a reputation for herself in the industry. But all of that changed one fateful day when she accidentally caused serious injury to a colleague on a construction site. The memory of the incident has haunted her ever since. The more Akua reflects on what happened, the more she becomes convinced that someone else would not have gotten into this situation (Self-Comparison). She feels isolated and set apart from others, as if she's living in a constant state of shame (Isolation). Her self-doubt has grown to the point where she barely recognizes herself anymore (Unrecognisable Self). These negative appraisals of herself have led Akua to develop maladaptive strategies to cope with her guilt. She's begun performing mental rituals, like counting steps or tapping her foot a certain number of times, in an attempt to prevent anything bad from happening again (Magical Prevention). When the rituals don't work, she resorts to self-blame rumination, dwelling on what she has done wrong and replaying the incident over and over in her mind. As Akua tries to make sense of her thoughts and emotions, she finds it difficult to deliberately recall the details of the incident (Hard to Recall Deliberately). When memories do surface, they're often accompanied by vivid sensory experiences – the taste of sweat on her lips, the sound of sirens blaring in the distance (Taste Vividness, Auditory Recall). These fragmented memories only serve to reinforce her negative appraisals of herself. She starts to wonder if she's truly capable of designing safe buildings or if she's just a menace waiting to happen. Akua's memories also trigger false alarms, making her react as if she's in danger even when there's no real threat (False Alarms). The sound of a car horn or the creaking of a floorboard is enough to startle her and send her heart racing. She becomes hypervigilant, constantly on the lookout for potential hazards that might not even exist. This state of heightened arousal makes it difficult for Akua to concentrate, and she finds herself struggling to focus on even the simplest tasks (Concentration). In an attempt to regain control, Akua resorts to downward comparison, reminding herself that things could have been worse (Downward Comparison). She tries to rationalize her way out of her guilt, but this only leads to more rumination and self-blame. Her mind becomes a vicious cycle of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and fragmented memories. As time goes on, Akua's relationships with her colleagues and loved ones begin to suffer. They notice the change in her demeanor – the constant checking and rechecking, the hesitation to take on new projects. They try to reassure her that it was an accident, but Akua can't shake off the feeling of responsibility. She starts to withdraw from social interactions, fearing that others will discover her "true" nature. It's only when Akua's husband sits her down and expresses his concern about her increasingly reclusive behavior that she realizes she needs help. The incident has left her with a deep-seated fear of causing harm to others, and she's desperate to break free from this cycle of guilt and self-doubt. As she begins therapy, Akua hopes to learn new ways to cope with her memories and negative appraisals, and to slowly rebuild her sense of self-worth as an architect and a person.
